# MCP agent check: 0.5.0

- **Release**: skforecast-ai 0.5.0, commit `9b3f74b`
- **Date**: 2026-10-29 15:32
- **Model**: `sonnet` (Claude Code 2.1.296, subscription, no API key)
- **Versions**: mcp 2.3.0, skforecast 0.27.0, Python 3.13.13
- **Sessions**: 90 finished, 0 pending; 12.35 USD equivalent (not a charge), 50.4 minutes

Fixed context:

| What the client loads | Characters | Tokens (about) |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Server instructions | 4,066 | 1,016 |
| Descriptions and schemas of the 11 tools | 31,958 | 7,990 |
| `SKILL.md`, when the agent loads it | 25,344 | 6,336 |
| Every session, client that defers tools (Claude Code): instructions, tool names, skill description | 4,832 | 1,208 |
| Every session, client that loads every tool: instructions, descriptions and schemas | 36,024 | 9,006 |

## Overall evaluation

Release run of 0.5.0 with `sonnet` (Claude Code 2.1.296), 25 scenarios, 3 repetitions and the ablation without the skill: 90 sessions, read by three reviewer agents with the rubric of the README. 63 correct, 26 improvable and 1 fail (`out_of_scope__r3`, not critical: asked for a grid search, it ran its own with `compare`). No critical scenario fails in any repetition. New in this release and read well: the Spanish Excel CSV (`excel_spanish`, 3 of 3 correct), numeric series ids (`numeric_ids`, 3 of 3), the cost confirmation (`expensive_run`: no run above the threshold and no `confirm_cost` before the user answered). The automatic check of the corrected copy in `dirty_data` and `dirty_data_keep_gaps` fails in most sessions because the client denies the shell command the agent writes the copy with, after the user agreed: a limit of the harness, judged by the reviewer on what the agent did.

## Findings

Written by the reviewer after reading 90 of the 90 sessions, most important first. Both lists are always present: an empty one says nothing was found.

### Problems of the library (server or skill)

6 found (to fix in skforecast-ai, then rerun the sessions).

| # | Finding | Cause | Sessions | Proposed action |
|--:|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | **After a plan with `use_exog: false`, `compare` without `candidates` ranks candidates that use the exogenous columns, and nothing in its response says that its winner needs future values.** In the 3 `exog_no_future` sessions with the skill, the agent builds the plan with `use_exog: false` at once (right), then calls `compare`. The rows named after a forecaster use `holiday`, `weather` and `temp`; only the row 'Strategy plan' leaves them out. The winner (ForecasterFoundation, MAE 30.94) uses them, and the response has 2 notices (license, metric unit), no `FutureExogNotice`. r1 calls `forecast` on `links.best_plan_id` and gets `invalid_argument` on `exog_path`, then follows the hint (a Foundation plan without exog, `backtest` on the same folds, MAE 37.51). r3 notices `Exogenous variables included` in the winner and runs a second `compare` with `use_exog: false` in each candidate. r2 runs a candidate `{}` (which takes the exogenous columns) and then a second `compare`. No data was written: 1 failed call and 3 extra comparisons. Confirmed by reading the code, not by a run: `strategy_candidate_config` carries `use_exog` only to the row 'Strategy plan', and `_exog_notices` is called only by `plan`, `refine_plan` and `forecast`, never by `compare`. | server | exog_no_future__r1, exog_no_future__r2, exog_no_future__r3 | When the plan of the strategy was built with `use_exog: false` by the user, either pass it to the candidates of `compare` without `candidates`, or add a `FutureExogNotice` to the response of `compare` naming the candidates (and the winner) that use exogenous columns and saying that `forecast` of `links.best_plan_id` needs `exog_path`. Step 6 of the skill already gives the workaround (`exog_columns: []`), and 0 of 3 agents used it. |
| 2 | **The summary of a strategy whose last fold is incomplete says only `12-step horizon, 6 folds`, and the agents describe every fold as complete.** h2o has 204 observations and the strategy trains on 142, so 62 values are tested: 5 folds of 12 and a last fold of 2. The summary gives `n_folds: 6`, `allow_incomplete_fold: True` and `12-step horizon, 6 folds`, and 12 sessions write `6 folds of 12 months each` or the like. The same in `multi_series`: 400 days, 280 of training, 9 folds of which the last has 8 days, written as `9 consecutive 14-day windows` in 3 of 3. Only `basic_forecast__noskill__r1` also gives the 62 months. Reproduced with `TimeSeriesFold(steps=12, initial_train_size=142, allow_incomplete_fold=True)` on 204 observations (6 folds, the last with 2) and with steps 14 and 280 on 400 (9 folds, the last with 8). | server | basic_forecast__r1, basic_forecast__r2, basic_forecast__r3, basic_forecast__noskill__r1, basic_forecast__noskill__r2, basic_forecast__noskill__r3, compare_code__r1, compare_code__r2, compare_code__r3, metric_list__r1, metric_list__r2, metric_list__r3, multi_series__r1, multi_series__r2, multi_series__r3 | In the `<deterministic_summary>` of `create_cv`, `backtest` and `compare`, say when the last fold is incomplete and how many observations it has (for example `6 folds, the last with 2 of 12 steps; 62 observations tested`). |
| 3 | **The fit counts of the cheaper strategies are computed by the agent, because the CostNotice names those strategies without their cost.** 6 of 6 expensive_run sessions quote in turn 1 a cost no response gives: `about 53` fits for refit=7 (r1, r3, noskill r1, noskill r2, noskill r3), `about 32` (r2), `about 13` for refit=30 (r1), `about 25` for every 15 days (noskill r1). They are n_folds divided by refit; every one the server later computed matches (53, 32, 13), so nothing wrong reached the user, but they are derived figures by the rule. The full text of the CostNotice (read in traces/expensive_run__r2.jsonl) lists `an integer refit`, `fewer folds` and `refit=false` with no number. | 4 | **compare says the plan of the strategy was not compared when a candidate sets an estimator argument to its default value, so the agent tells the user the default plan is absent while it is the winner.** out_of_scope__r3: candidate ridge_a1 is Ridge with estimator_kwargs {"alpha": 1}, the scikit-learn default, and the default plan has estimator_kwargs {}. compare answers with the UserWarning 'The plan the strategy was created for (ForecasterRecursive + Ridge) makes other decisions than every candidate, so it was not compared'. ridge_a1 scores MAE 0.061982, exactly the row ForecasterRecursive / Ridge of the default compare on the same file and folds in probe_why_winner__r1 to r3. This text feeds the context of ask(), so it needs the paid check of /llm-context-change. |
| 5 | **dayfirst_dates no longer exercises what it was written for: profile reads the day-first dates without a notice, and no answer can tell the user the order it used.** The file holds 200 days written %d/%m/%Y from 01/01/2024 (generator _dayfirst in check_mcp_agent.py). In 3 of 3 sessions profile returns 0 notices, Date range 2024-01-01 to 2024-07-18 and no irregularities: read right, in silence, as the skill says for dates with a day after the 12th. The expected text ('notices the notice or the error about the format of the dates and tells the user') has nothing to act on, and the check 'the answer talks about the dates' passes on the word 'dates' only. No session mentions the day-first format; none could, since the summary of the profile does not say which order it read. | server | dayfirst_dates__r1, dayfirst_dates__r2, dayfirst_dates__r3 | Either add a line to the dataset summary of profile with the date format it read (for example 'Dates: written day first, read as such') so the agent can confirm it, or rewrite the scenario with monthly data on the first of each month, which still raises the DataProfileWarning or the error that asks for dayfirst, and update its expected text. |
| 6 | **With intervals estimated from few residuals, two of three agents relabel the interval at the coverage measured on 24 values, and the third derives a count.** interval_few_residuals: create_cv warns that the intervals rest on 24 residuals and tend to be too narrow; backtest gives coverage 0.7083 of 24 actual values, with no IntervalCoverageNotice. All 3 sessions tell the user about the warning. r1 writes 'should be read as roughly 70% coverage, not 80%' and r3 'I'd quote it as roughly a 71% interval rather than an 80% one', presenting a coverage measured on 24 values over 2 folds as the reliable level, which is what the scenario asks to avoid. r2 says the opposite (not a precise figure) but adds '17 of 24', a count no response gives, and 'within what chance could produce', a statistical claim of its own. The skill tells the agent to give the measured coverage instead of the nominal level when an IntervalCoverageNotice says it is clearly below, and to report the measured coverage with the interval; it says nothing about a coverage measured on few values, and the few-residuals warning is not repeated by backtest. | skill | interval_few_residuals__r1, interval_few_residuals__r2, interval_few_residuals__r3 | Add to the interval paragraph of the skill: the coverage of a backtest is measured on n_folds x steps values; with few of them (or after a warning that the intervals rest on few residuals) report it as measured on that number of values and do not restate the interval at that level. Optionally repeat the few-residuals warning in the response of backtest, which the 0.4.0 log already noted it does not do. |

13 found (the library gave the right information and the agent did not use it well).

Yet `basic_forecast__r2` opens with `its uncertainty band is probably a bit too narrow`, `basic_forecast__noskill__r2` with `its stated uncertainty band is probably a little too narrow` and `the true uncertainty may be somewhat larger than the bounds show`, and `basic_forecast__noskill__r3` with `its 80% interval is probably too narrow`, while each of them later says the interval held up. Nothing in a response supports it. 3 of 6 `basic_forecast` sessions, with and without the skill. | model | basic_forecast__r2, basic_forecast__noskill__r2, basic_forecast__noskill__r3 | No change of rule is needed (the skill and the instructions forbid statements nothing supports). ### Final answer

> ## Forecast for x, July 2008 to June 2009
>
> I used the Chronos-2-small foundation model, which had the lowest error in the comparison. The data is monthly, 204 observations from 1991-07 to 2008-06, with no gaps or missing values. Its license is Apache-2.0, and it downloads weights on first use.
>
> | Month | Forecast | 80% interval (nominal) |
> |---|---|---|
> | 2008-07 | 1.003 | 0.929 – 1.077 |
> | 2008-08 | 1.031 | 0.943 – 1.107 |
> | 2008-09 | 1.084 | 0.996 – 1.166 |
> | 2008-10 | 1.184 | 1.086 – 1.282 |
> | 2008-11 | 1.171 | 1.076 – 1.261 |
> | 2008-12 | 1.281 | 1.170 – 1.389 |
> | 2009-01 | 1.281 | 1.169 – 1.394 |
> | 2009-02 | 0.682 | 0.612 – 0.756 |
> | 2009-03 | 0.791 | 0.720 – 0.865 |
> | 2009-04 | 0.761 | 0.691 – 0.835 |
> | 2009-05 | 0.844 | 0.764 – 0.924 |
> | 2009-06 | 0.912 | 0.826 – 1.000 |
>
> ## Can you trust it?
>
> **Partly.** The forecast itself has no error measure. The evidence comes from a backtest of the same model: 6 folds of 12 months each, covering 2003-04 to 2008-06. The model was trained once on data up to 2003-04.
>
> - **Better than the baseline:** Chronos-2 had a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0570. The seasonal naive baseline, which repeats last year's values, scored 0.0661. Three of the four candidates beat the baseline. The exception was ForecasterDirect with Ridge, at 0.0763.
> - **Close ranking:** ForecasterStats (Arima) was second at 0.0607, and ForecasterRecursive with Ridge was third at 0.0620. The gap between the top three is small. Only 6 folds measured it, so the exact order is not firmly established.
> - **Scaled error below 1:** The mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for Chronos-2 was 0.579. That is below the one-step naive forecast (repeat the previous value). It is not a comparison against the seasonal baseline.
> - **Interval coverage:** The 80% interval covered 79.0% of actual values in the backtest, so it looks reasonably calibrated. The interval is narrow, with a mean width of 0.182 in the units of x. The backtest only measured 62 values.
> - **Weaker candidates:** The Ridge-based candidates covered only 64.5% (ForecasterRecursive) and 58.1% (ForecasterDirect). I did not use them for the forecast.
>
> The backtest used a single training of the Ridge-based candidates. The backtest is also not a guarantee for the next 12 months.
>
> I can export a reproducible script with `get_code` if you want one.

### Final answer

> **Short answer:** The forecast is reasonably trustworthy, but it has been measured on only 6 folds and its uncertainty band is probably a bit too narrow.
>
> ## Forecast for x, July 2008 to June 2009
> The data is monthly, with 204 observations from 1991-07 to 2008-06, no gaps and no missing values. The model is Chronos-2 small (Apache-2.0 licence, as the server reports it). The interval is nominally 80%.
>
> | Month | Forecast | Interval (10%–90%) |
> |---|---|---|
> | 2008-07 | 1.003 | 0.929 – 1.077 |
> | 2008-08 | 1.031 | 0.943 – 1.107 |
> | 2008-09 | 1.084 | 0.996 – 1.166 |
> | 2008-10 | 1.184 | 1.086 – 1.282 |
> | 2008-11 | 1.171 | 1.076 – 1.261 |
> | 2008-12 | 1.281 | 1.170 – 1.389 |
> | 2009-01 | 1.281 | 1.169 – 1.394 |
> | 2009-02 | 0.682 | 0.612 – 0.756 |
> | 2009-03 | 0.791 | 0.720 – 0.865 |
> | 2009-04 | 0.761 | 0.691 – 0.835 |
> | 2009-05 | 0.844 | 0.764 – 0.924 |
> | 2009-06 | 0.912 | 0.826 – 1.000 |
>
> ## Can you trust it?
> I compared five configurations over 6 backtest folds of 12 months each, with training up to 2003-04. This is the strongest check the server offers. Lower error is better.
>
> | Candidate | MAE | MASE | Interval coverage (nominal 80%) |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | **Chronos-2 (chosen)** | 0.0570 | 0.579 | 79.0% |
> | ARIMA | 0.0607 | 0.616 | 74.2% |
> | Ridge, recursive | 0.0620 | 0.672 | 64.5% |
> | Seasonal naive baseline | 0.0661 | 0.729 | 75.8% |
> | Ridge, direct | 0.0763 | 0.827 | 58.1% |
>
> - **It beats the baseline.** Three of the four candidates beat the seasonal naive baseline, and Chronos-2 had the lowest error. Its MAE of 0.0570 compares with 0.0661 for the baseline, on a series whose values run from 0.34 to 1.26.
> - **MASE is below 1.** That means it beats a one-step naive forecast on the training data. It is not a comparison with the seasonal baseline.
> - **The interval is roughly calibrated for the chosen model.** It covered 79.0% of actual values against the 80% target, so the bands are about as honest as they claim. The server's notice flags the two Ridge models, not this one.
>
> ## Caveats
> - **The margin is small.** Chronos-2 and ARIMA are close (0.0570 vs 0.0607), and 6 folds is a short record. Treat the ranking as suggestive, not settled.
> - **The forecast itself has no error measure.** The figures above come from the backtest of the same plan, not from the forecast of the future.
> - **The model was not retrained per fold.** Only ARIMA and the foundation model use data up to each fold. The Ridge models were trained once, so their rows are not like-for-like.
> - **I haven't looked at the data's behaviour beyond the profile.** The server does not explain why a model wins or why the forecast has its shape, so I won't speculate. The sharp drop from January to February 2009 (1.281 to 0.682) is what the model predicts, but I can't say why.
>
> I can also give you the reproducible script (`get_code`), or re-run with a longer backtest (e.g. refitting each fold) if you want a firmer accuracy estimate.

**LLM (answer of turn 1, under "Final answer")**

### Final answer

> I forecast the next 12 months (2008-07 to 2009-06) with the best-scoring model, and it's moderately trustworthy. It beat a seasonal-naive baseline in a 6-fold backtest, but that margin is modest.
>
> **Forecast** (Chronos-2-small foundation model, no training; Apache-2.0 license per the server)
>
> | Month | Forecast | 80% interval (nominal) |
> |---|---|---|
> | 2008-07 | 1.003 | 0.929 – 1.077 |
> | 2008-08 | 1.031 | 0.943 – 1.107 |
> | 2008-09 | 1.084 | 0.996 – 1.166 |
> | 2008-10 | 1.184 | 1.086 – 1.282 |
> | 2008-11 | 1.171 | 1.076 – 1.261 |
> | 2008-12 | 1.281 | 1.170 – 1.389 |
> | 2009-01 | 1.281 | 1.169 – 1.394 |
> | 2009-02 | 0.682 | 0.612 – 0.756 |
> | 2009-03 | 0.791 | 0.720 – 0.865 |
> | 2009-04 | 0.761 | 0.691 – 0.835 |
> | 2009-05 | 0.844 | 0.764 – 0.924 |
> | 2009-06 | 0.912 | 0.826 – 1.000 |
>
> The data is monthly, 204 observations from 1991-07 to 2008-06, with no gaps or missing values.
>
> **How far to trust it**
>
> The backtest used 6 folds of 12 months each, with initial training up to 2003-04. I compared five models against a seasonal-naive baseline, which repeats last year's values. Lower error is better.
>
> | Model | MAE | Beats baseline? |
> |---|---|---|
> | Chronos-2-small (used) | 0.0570 | yes |
> | ARIMA | 0.0607 | yes |
> | Ridge, recursive | 0.0620 | yes |
> | Seasonal-naive baseline | 0.0661 | – |
> | Ridge, direct | 0.0763 | no |
>
> - **Beats the baseline:** 3 of the 4 models did, and Chronos was the best. The server reports it as 13.7% ahead of the baseline and 6.0% ahead of ARIMA.
> - **Not a large margin:** the gap to ARIMA and Ridge is small, and 6 folds is a short sample. Treat the ranking as indicative.
> - **Typical error:** Chronos averaged about 0.057 per month, with a root mean squared error of 0.073, on a series that ranges from 0.34 to 1.26.
> - **Interval:** the Chronos 80% interval covered 79% of actual values in the backtest, so it is roughly calibrated. That is a measurement over 62 values, so treat it as an estimate. The ARIMA interval covered 74%.
> - **Weaker intervals:** the two Ridge models fell clearly short of 80%, at 65% and 58%. I didn't use them.
> - **Future check:** a forecast of the future has no error measure of its own. The numbers above come from past folds and may not carry over to 2008-07 onward.
>
> I haven't saved a script. `get_code` can give you one to reproduce this outside the server.

### Final answer

> I forecast `x` for July 2008 to June 2009. The backtest says the forecast is reasonably trustworthy for the point estimate, but the intervals are the weaker part.
>
> **Forecast**
> - The model is Chronos-2-small (Apache-2.0), a pretrained foundation model that needs no training.
> - Predictions range from 0.68 to 1.28 and average about 1.00.
> - The 80% interval averages about 0.92 to 1.09.
> - The full 12 rows, with bounds, are in `out/forecast-6-4a9faf-predictions.csv`.
>
> **Can you trust it?**
> I compared five models over 6 backtest folds of 12 months each. Training ended in April 2003, and the folds cover the 62 months from May 2003 to the end of the data.
>
> | Model | MAE | MASE |
> |---|---|---|
> | Chronos-2 (used) | 0.0570 | 0.58 |
> | Auto-ARIMA | 0.0607 | 0.62 |
> | Ridge, recursive | 0.0620 | 0.67 |
> | Seasonal naive baseline | 0.0661 | 0.73 |
> | Ridge, direct | 0.0763 | 0.83 |
>
> - **Beats the baseline:** Chronos-2 has the lowest error, 13.7% below the seasonal naive baseline.
> - **Beats one-step naive:** its MASE is below 1.
> - **Typical error:** about ±0.057 on a series whose mean is 0.77 (MAPE about 6.7%).
> - **Small margin:** the gap between Chronos-2 and Auto-ARIMA is only 6%. With 6 folds on one series, I wouldn't call that margin decisive.
> - **Intervals:** the 80% interval covered 79% of actual values in the backtest, so it is about right for Chronos-2. The Ridge intervals covered much less (65% and 58%), which matters only if you switch to those models.
> - **Data checks:** the data had no missing values or irregular dates, and there were no data warnings.
>
> **Caveats**
> - A forecast of the future has no error measure of its own. The numbers above come from past folds and assume the next year behaves like 2003–2008.
> - The backtest did not refit the models between folds, except Auto-ARIMA, which refits every fold.
> - I did not tune any hyperparameters, because this tool only compares the candidates it is given.

### Final answer

> I forecast x for July 2008 to June 2009 with Chronos-2-small, a pre-trained foundation model. It was the best of five candidates in a backtest. The forecast looks reasonably trustworthy, but its stated uncertainty band is probably a little too narrow.
>
> **Forecast**
> - The 12 predictions average about 1.00. They range from about 0.68 to 1.28.
> - The model's 80% interval has a mean width of about 0.18 in the backtest.
> - The predictions, with lower and upper bounds, are in `/private/var/folders/wt/8tvn563d5v55nspfbydgqb9r0000gp/T/skfast_mcp_97sxh5ey/out/forecast-6-f84dc0-predictions.csv`. The path is `.../out/forecast-6-f84dc0-predictions.csv` under the working directory.
>
> **Data**
> - The series is monthly, 204 observations from 1991-07 to 2008-06, with no missing values or irregular dates.
> - It has no exogenous columns, so nothing from outside the series was used.
>
> **Backtest evidence**
> I backtested on 6 consecutive 12-month windows, with training up to 2003-04. Lower mean absolute error (MAE) is better.
>
> | Model | MAE | Interval coverage (target 80%) |
> |---|---|---|
> | Chronos-2-small (chosen) | 0.0570 | 79% |
> | ARIMA | 0.0607 | 74% |
> | Ridge (recursive) | 0.0620 | 65% |
> | Seasonal naive baseline | 0.0661 | 76% |
> | Ridge (direct) | 0.0763 | 58% |
>
> - **Beats the baseline:** Chronos beat the seasonal-naive baseline in this backtest. That is the strongest evidence I can give you.
> - **Margin is small:** Chronos led ARIMA, the runner-up, by only 0.0037 MAE, so the ranking among the top three is not decisive.
> - **Typical error:** the average miss was about 0.057 per month, with a root mean squared error of 0.073. The series has a standard deviation of 0.225.
> - **Scaled error:** the mean absolute scaled error was 0.58. That is below 1, so it beat the one-step naive forecast on the training data.
>
> **Caveats**
> - **Interval:** Chronos's interval covered 79% of actual values in the backtest, close to the nominal 80%. That was measured over only 62 values, so treat it as approximate. Even so, the true uncertainty may be somewhat larger than the bounds show.
> - **Limited test:** the backtest covers 6 windows, all from 2003 to 2008. It says nothing about whether the series will change behaviour after 2008.
> - **No error measure for the future:** the forecast of the future itself has no error measure. The accuracy figures above come from past windows.
> - **License:** Chronos-2-small is Apache-2.0 licensed.

### Final answer

> I forecast x for July 2008 to June 2009. The forecast is reasonably trustworthy, but its 80% interval is probably too narrow.
>
> **The forecast**
> - The model is Chronos-2-small, a pre-trained foundation model under the Apache-2.0 license. It ranked first in the comparison below.
> - The forecast values average about 1.00 over the 12 months. They run from about 0.68 at the lowest to 1.28 at the highest.
> - Each month has an 80% interval. The lower bounds average about 0.92 and the upper bounds about 1.09.
> - All 12 months, with bounds, are in `out/forecast-6-52d046-predictions.csv`.
>
> **Can you trust it?**
> I backtested 6 yearly folds, each a 12-month window, with training up to April 2003. I compared the model against four alternatives and a seasonal-naive baseline, which repeats last year's values:
>
> | Model | MAE | Coverage of 80% interval |
> |---|---|---|
> | Chronos-2-small (chosen) | 0.0570 | 79% |
> | Auto-ARIMA | 0.0607 | 74% |
> | Ridge, recursive | 0.0620 | 65% |
> | Seasonal naive baseline | 0.0661 | 76% |
> | Ridge, direct | 0.0763 | 58% |
>
> - **It beats the baseline.** Chronos has the lowest error, 13.7% below the seasonal-naive baseline. Its MASE is 0.579, which beats the one-step naive forecast.
> - **The edge is modest.** It is only 6.0% ahead of ARIMA. With 6 folds, I wouldn't read much into the gap between the top three models.
> - **Its interval held up.** Its 80% interval covered 79% of the actual values in the backtest, so the bounds look about right.
> - **The ranking isn't a guarantee.** The backtest trained once with no refit, and it ran on only 62 actual values. The forecast itself has no error measure of its own. The backtest error is the best guide to how far off it may be.
>
> The Ridge models' intervals covered clearly less than 80%, but I didn't use those models.
>
> The backtest says nothing about changes after June 2008. A shift in the series would not show up in these numbers.

### Final answer

> I forecast `users` for the 24 hours from 2012-12-31 00:00 to 23:00. Across the forecast, predicted users range from about 9.8 to 333.1 per hour, with a mean of about 125.1. The hourly values are in `out/forecast-8-5deb22-predictions.csv`.

> - **Model:** It is Chronos-2-small, a pre-trained foundation model (Apache-2.0 license). It downloads its weights the first time it runs and needs no training.
>
> **How accurate it is**
> - **Comparison, with exogenous columns included:** I compared candidates on 27 daily folds (24-hour forecasts). Chronos-2-small had the lowest mean absolute error, 30.9 users. The comparison also ran two LightGBM-based forecasters and a seasonal-naive baseline, which repeats the previous day. 3 of the 4 configurations beat the baseline's error of 54.7. The plan I started from, a recursive LightGBM, did not beat it (59.8).
> - **Backtest of the plan I actually used:** I re-measured Chronos-2-small without the exogenous columns on the same folds. Its mean absolute error was 37.5 users, with a root mean squared error of 62.7. That is the figure that applies to this forecast.
> - **No baseline for the final plan:** I did not run the seasonal-naive baseline for this version.
> - **No interval:** I did not request a prediction interval, so there is no uncertainty range on the forecast.

> - **Negative predictions:** some backtest predictions went slightly below zero, with a minimum of about -2.
> - **Forecast error:** the forecast of the future has no error measure of its own. The backtest figures are the best guide to its accuracy.

### Final answer

> I forecast `users` for 2012-12-31 00:00 to 23:00 (24 hourly steps). The predicted values are in `<ws>/out/forecast-5-07202e-predictions.csv`. I haven't opened that file, so I can't give you the hour-by-hour numbers here.

>
> **Model**
> - It is a `ForecasterRecursive` with an `LGBMRegressor` estimator, which are the server's recommended defaults.
> - It uses 29 lags, rolling means over 3, 24 and 168 hours, and a rolling standard deviation over 3 hours.
> - It also uses hour, day-of-week and weekend features.
> - It uses `holiday`, `weather` and `temp` as predictors, with their future values taken from `data/bike_next_24h.csv`.
>
> **Accuracy**
> - I backtested the same plan over 27 daily folds, covering 2012-12-04 to 2012-12-30.
> - The model was trained once and not refit in each fold.
> - Mean absolute error was 44.1 users, and root mean squared error was 72.2 users.
> - Mean absolute scaled error was 0.54, which is below the one-step naive forecast of repeating the previous hour.
> - Mean absolute percentage error was 124.5%. It is inflated because some hours have very low user counts.
> - I did not run a `compare` against the seasonal baseline, so I can't say whether this model beats a seasonal naive forecast.
> - The forecast of the future itself has no error measure of its own.

### Final answer

> I forecast the 24 hours of 2012-12-31 (00:00 to 23:00) for `users`. The predictions have a mean of about 63.8 users per hour, a minimum of 7.3 and a maximum of 151.7. The 24 hourly values are in `out/forecast-4-323b55-predictions.csv`.
>
> **Model:** I used the server's recommended setup, a recursive LightGBM forecaster. It uses lags up to 169 hours, rolling means over 3, 24 and 168 hours, and a rolling standard deviation over 3 hours. It also uses hour, day-of-week and weekend features, plus `holiday`, `weather` and `temp`. The future values of those three columns come from your `bike_next_24h.csv`.
>
> **Accuracy (backtest):** I backtested the same plan over 27 consecutive 24-hour folds, covering 2012-12-04 to 2012-12-30. The model was trained once, on data up to 2012-12-03.
>
> | Metric | Value |
> |---|---|
> | Mean absolute error | 44.1 users per hour |
> | Root mean squared error | 72.2 users per hour |
> | Mean absolute scaled error | 0.54 |
> | Mean absolute percentage error | 124.5% |
>
> - **Scaled error:** a value below 1 beats repeating the previous hour's value. It is not a comparison against a seasonal naive forecast.
> - **Percentage error:** it is inflated by hours with very low counts, since the target goes as low as 1.
> - **No baseline comparison:** I did not run `compare`, so I can't say how the model does against a seasonal baseline or other candidates.
> - **No intervals:** the plan had no prediction interval, so the forecast is a single value per hour.

**LLM (answer of turn 1, under "Final answer")**

### Final answer

> I forecast the next 14 days (2015-01-02 to 2015-01-15) for item_1, item_2 and item_3. The best model beats the naive forecast for item_1 and item_3 but only matches it for item_2. I assumed `date`, `series` and `value` were the date, item and sales columns, since the file has no others.
>
> ## Method
> I compared two models over 9 backtest folds of 14 days each. The winner was Chronos-2 (`autogluon/chronos-2-small`), a pre-trained foundation model with an Apache-2.0 license. It had a lower error than the gradient-boosting model (LightGBM) the server recommends by default (MASE 0.79 against 1.11). Only those two candidates ran, and the comparison has no seasonal-naive baseline for several series. MASE measures error against a "repeat yesterday" forecast, and below 1 means better than that.
>
> The measured error comes from the backtest, not from the forecast itself. The forecast of the future has no error measure of its own.
>
> ## Forecast
> The full daily values and bounds are in `out/forecast-7-aa9abb-predictions.csv`.
>
> | Item | Forecast range | Mean | Starts at | Ends at |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | item_1 | 14.2 – 20.1 | 17.0 | 14.2 | 19.8 |
> | item_2 | 19.5 – 20.2 | 19.8 | 19.7 | 20.2 |
> | item_3 | 20.2 – 21.7 | 21.0 | 20.2 | 21.3 |
>
> item_1 starts lower than its history (mean about 22) and climbs back toward 20 over the 14 days. item_2 and item_3 are nearly flat.
>
> ## Reliability per item (Chronos-2 backtest)
>
> | Item | MAE | MASE | Interval coverage (80% nominal) | Reliability |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | item_1 | 0.91 | 0.60 | 82.5% | **Best.** It clearly beats the naive forecast. |
> | item_3 | 2.97 | 0.77 | 85% | **Moderate.** It beats the naive forecast, but absolute errors are larger. |
> | item_2 | 2.52 | 1.00 | 85% | **Weakest.** It is no better than repeating the previous day's value. |
>
> - **Prediction intervals:** the 80% intervals (10th to 90th percentile) covered 82.5–85% of actual values in the backtest, close to their nominal level. They are estimates, and they are wide (mean width 2.6 for item_1, 8.8 for item_2 and 11.6 for item_3). For item_2 and item_3, treat the point forecast as a rough central value.
> - **LightGBM:** I don't recommend its forecast. Its intervals covered only 27.5–35% of actual values, far below the 80% they claim, so its uncertainty is understated. Its error was also higher for every item.
> - **item_2 and item_3:** these are the items to be most careful with. item_2 has the highest MASE (1.00), and item_3 has the largest absolute errors.
>
> The first run downloads the Chronos-2 weights from Hugging Face. I can pull the reproducible script with `get_code` if you want it.

### Final answer

> I forecast 2015-01-02 to 2015-01-15 for the three items. The model only partly beats a naive "repeat yesterday" forecast, and the 80% prediction intervals are too narrow, so treat all three forecasts as rough.
>
> **Method:** one LightGBM model for the three items, with 6 lags, rolling-window features and calendar features. The data has 400 days per item, from 2013-11-28 to 2015-01-01, with no gaps or missing values. I assumed `date`, `series` and `value` were the date, item and sales columns, since you didn't name them.
>
> **Reliability:** I tested the model on 9 consecutive 14-day windows. The MASE below compares its error with a naive forecast that repeats the previous day. Below 1 is better than naive and above 1 is worse.
>
> | Item | Mean abs. error | MASE | Forecast mean (14 days) | Forecast range | Interval coverage (target 80%) |
> |---|---|---|---|---|---|
> | item_1 | 1.55 | 0.97 | 24.5 | 18.6–29.0 | 35% |
> | item_2 | 3.12 | 1.36 | 20.7 | 18.3–23.8 | 27.5% |
> | item_3 | 3.68 | 1.01 | 20.6 | 17.4–22.9 | 32.5% |
>
> - **item_1 is the most reliable.** It has the lowest absolute error and is the only item slightly better than naive (MASE 0.97).
> - **item_3 is about the same as naive** (MASE 1.01), and its error is the largest in absolute terms.
> - **item_2 is the least reliable.** Its MASE of 1.36 means the model did worse than repeating the previous day.
> - **The intervals are not trustworthy.** I asked for 80% intervals, but in the backtest the real values fell inside them only 27.5–35% of the time. The uncertainty is larger than the bounds suggest. I haven't read the interval rows, so I'm not quoting them. They are in `out/forecast-5-92d3e7-predictions.csv`.
>
> **Limits:**
> - I didn't run a comparison against a seasonal-naive baseline or other models. The only reference is the one-step naive forecast inside MASE. So I can't say whether a different model would do better, especially for item_2.
> - The forecast of the future has no error measure of its own. The accuracy figures come from the backtest of the same model.
> - The model was trained once and not refit during the backtest. It was trained on the first 280 days (to 2014-09-03) and tested on the remaining 120 days.
>
> The point forecasts for each day are in the predictions file above. I can run a comparison of several models next, which is cheap here, to see whether any beats this one on item_2.

**LLM (answer of turn 1, under "Final answer")**

### Final answer

> I forecast the 14 days from 2015-01-02 to 2015-01-15 for all three items. The forecasts are only weakly reliable, and the 80% intervals are not trustworthy.
>
> I used one LightGBM model across the three items (ForecasterRecursiveMultiSeries). I did not set `use_exog`, but the file has no other columns, so it used only each item's own sales history. The daily values and the bounds for each day are in `out/forecast-5-12b5bd-predictions.csv`.
>
> ## Forecast (average over the 14 days)
>
> | Item | Mean | Min | Max |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | item_1 | 24.53 | 18.56 | 28.96 |
> | item_2 | 20.70 | 18.31 | 23.76 |
> | item_3 | 20.59 | 17.38 | 22.87 |
>
> ## Reliability
>
> I backtested the model on 9 consecutive 14-day windows, from 2014-09-04 to 2015-01-01. The model was trained once and not refit between windows.
>
> | Item | MAE (units of sales) | MASE | Reading |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | item_1 | 1.55 | 0.97 | Most reliable, but barely better than repeating the previous day's value. |
> | item_3 | 3.68 | 1.01 | About the same as repeating the previous day's value. Its errors are the largest in absolute terms. |
> | item_2 | 3.12 | 1.36 | Least reliable. It does worse than repeating the previous day's value. |
>
> - **MASE:** it compares the error to a one-step "repeat yesterday" forecast on the training data. Below 1 is better than that, above 1 is worse. The average across items is 1.11, so on this measure the model is not clearly better than a trivial forecast.
> - **Baseline:** the server gives no seasonal-naive baseline comparison for multi-series data, so I can't say how the model does against that.
> - **Prediction intervals:** the 80% intervals covered the actual values only 35% of the time for item_1, 27.5% for item_2 and 32.5% for item_3. The real uncertainty is much larger than the bounds in the forecast file show. Don't use them as 80% ranges.
>
> I only ran the default plan and did not compare other models. The server can compare candidate configurations (for example Ridge, XGBoost or a foundation model) on the same windows if you want to see whether any does better, especially for item_2.

````text
import pandas as pd
from skforecast.foundation import FoundationModel, ForecasterFoundation

# Load data
data = pd.read_csv('<ws>/data/h2o.csv')

data['fecha'] = pd.to_datetime(data['fecha'])
data = data.set_index('fecha')
data = data.asfreq('MS')
data = data.sort_index()

series = data['x']

# Create foundation model (chronos-2-small)
estimator = FoundationModel(
    model_id       = 'autogluon/chronos-2-small',
    context_length = 8192,
)

# Create forecaster
forecaster = ForecasterFoundation(estimator=estimator)

# Fit (stores context only, no training)
forecaster.fit(series=series)

# Predict
steps = 12
predictions = forecaster.predict(steps=steps)
print(predictions)

````

### Final answer

> **Best model: Chronos-2 small (`ForecasterFoundation`, `autogluon/chronos-2-small`).** It had the lowest error in the comparison. I forecast `x` for the next 12 months, 2008-07 to 2009-06.
>
> **How I compared them.** I used a 6-fold backtest with 12-month folds. Training ended at 2003-04-01 for the first fold. The ranking metric was mean absolute error (MAE).
>
> | Rank | Model | MAE | RMSE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 1 | Chronos-2 small (foundation model) | 0.0570 | 0.0726 |
> | 2 | Auto-ARIMA (`ForecasterStats`) | 0.0607 | 0.0790 |
> | 3 | Recursive Ridge | 0.0620 | 0.0766 |
> | 4 | Seasonal naive baseline | 0.0661 | 0.0816 |
> | 5 | Direct Ridge | 0.0763 | 0.0958 |
>
> - **Against the baseline:** 3 of the 4 models beat the seasonal naive baseline. Only Direct Ridge did not.
> - **Forecast values:** the predictions have a minimum of 0.682, a maximum of 1.281 and a mean of 1.002. The 12 monthly values are in `out/forecast-6-38a7e6-predictions.csv`.
> - **Accuracy:** the forecast of the future has no error measure of its own. The backtest above is the accuracy evidence.
> - **Data and cost:** there were no data problems. The comparison was cheap, so no cost confirmation was needed.
> - **License and download:** Chronos-2 small is licensed Apache-2.0. It downloads its weights from Hugging Face the first time you run it.
> - **Prediction interval:** I didn't request one.
> - **Margin over ARIMA:** Chronos's lead over Auto-ARIMA is small.
>
> **Script.** It is exactly what the server generated, with the data path as the only absolute path in it:
>
> ```python
> import pandas as pd
> from skforecast.foundation import FoundationModel, ForecasterFoundation
>
> # Load data
> data = pd.read_csv('<ws>/data/h2o.csv')
>
> data['fecha'] = pd.to_datetime(data['fecha'])
> data = data.set_index('fecha')
> data = data.asfreq('MS')
> data = data.sort_index()
>
> series = data['x']
>
> # Create foundation model (chronos-2-small)
> estimator = FoundationModel(
>     model_id       = 'autogluon/chronos-2-small',
>     context_length = 8192,
> )
>
> # Create forecaster
> forecaster = ForecasterFoundation(estimator=estimator)
>
> # Fit (stores context only, no training)
> forecaster.fit(series=series)
>
> # Predict
> steps = 12
> predictions = forecaster.predict(steps=steps)
> print(predictions)
> ```
>
> Change the `read_csv` path if your copy of `h2o.csv` is somewhere else.
>
> **Install:**
> ```
> pip install pandas==2.3.3 skforecast==0.27.0 chronos-forecasting==2.3.2
> ```

### Final answer

> I ran the backtest and the 24-hour forecast. The 80% interval is too narrow to trust at that level.
>
> **Setup**
> - The data is hourly `users`, 2,160 rows from 2012-10-02 to 2012-12-30 23:00, with no gaps or missing values.
> - The model is a `ForecasterRecursive` with `LGBMRegressor`. I used the 48 lags and MAE you asked for, and an 80% interval (`[0.1, 0.9]`, bootstrapped).
> - The server's rules added three window features (rolling means over 3, 24 and 168 hours, plus a 3-hour rolling standard deviation) and calendar features (hour, day of week, weekend).
> - The backtest used 27 folds of 24 hours each, covering 2012-12-04 to 2012-12-30. The model was trained once, on data up to 2012-12-03 23:00.
>
> **Backtest**
> - **MAE:** 66.24 users per hour. The series averages 216 users per hour.
> - **Interval coverage:** only 43.4% of the 648 actual values fell inside the nominal 80% interval. The mean interval width was 107.4 users.
> - The server flagged this with an `IntervalCoverageNotice`. The real uncertainty is larger than the bounds show.
> - The backtest has no baseline, so I can't say how much better it is than a simple forecast.
>
> **Forecast for 2012-12-31 00:00 to 23:00**
> - **Point predictions:** they range from 6.2 to 199.1 users per hour, with a mean of 89.0.
> - **Bounds:** the lower bound averages 32.4 and the upper bound averages 133.4.
> - **What to rely on:** the MAE above is the accuracy measure. A forecast of the future has no error measure of its own.
> - **Interval caveat:** treat the bounds as roughly 43% intervals, not 80%.
>
> Files are in `<ws>/out/`:
> - `forecast-5-659190-predictions.csv`
> - `backtest-4-659190-predictions.csv`
> - `backtest-4-659190-metrics.csv`
>
> I can run a `compare` against the seasonal baseline and other candidates, or generate the reproducible script.

### Final answer

> I compared five models for a 12-month horizon on `x` in `data/h2o.csv`. The data is monthly, 204 observations from 1991-07 to 2008-06, with no gaps or missing values. The ranking is by MSE, with MAE alongside.
>
> | Rank | Model | MSE | MAE |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 1 | Chronos-2 small (foundation model) | 0.005272 | 0.057007 |
> | 2 | Recursive forecaster with Ridge | 0.005863 | 0.061982 |
> | 3 | Auto-ARIMA | 0.006240 | 0.060668 |
> | 4 | Seasonal naive baseline | 0.006663 | 0.066072 |
> | 5 | Direct forecaster with Ridge | 0.009176 | 0.076281 |
>
> - **Winner:** Chronos-2 small has the lowest MSE and the lowest MAE. It is the only model that is not trained. Its license is Apache-2.0, and it downloads its weights from Hugging Face the first time it runs.
> - **Against the baseline:** 3 of the 4 models beat the seasonal naive baseline on MSE. The direct Ridge forecaster does not.
> - **MAE order:** Auto-ARIMA has a lower MAE than the recursive Ridge model, although its MSE is higher, so the two metrics order those two models differently.
> - **Backtest setup:** The backtest has 6 folds of 12 months each. The first training window ends 2003-04-01, which is 70% of the data. The Ridge models were trained once. Auto-ARIMA was refitted in every fold, and Chronos-2 is never trained.
> - **Cost:** The comparison used 19 estimator fits, under the 50-fit threshold.
>
> I haven't produced the actual 12-month forecast yet. I can run it with the winning plan (`plan-5-337e62`) if you want. A forecast of the future carries no error measure of its own, so the backtest figures above are the accuracy estimate.

### Final answer

**Turn 1**

> I haven't run the backtest yet. Retraining before every daily forecast would take 366 model fits, which is above the server's 50-fit threshold, so I need you to choose how to run it.
>
> **Setup so far**
> - **Data:** 17,544 hourly observations of `users`, 2011-01-01 to 2012-12-31. There are no missing values or gaps and no exogenous columns.
> - **Model:** the server's recommended LightGBM recursive forecaster with a 24-step horizon. Its primary metric is MAE.
> - **Backtest design (my choice):** train on 2011 and test on all of 2012. Each fold forecasts the next 24 hours, then the model retrains on all data up to that point. That gives 366 daily folds.
>
> **Options**
>
> | Option | Estimator fits |
> |---|---|
> | Retrain every day (as designed above) | 366 |
> | Retrain weekly (`refit=7`) | about 53, so likely still above the threshold and needing confirmation |
> | Retrain monthly (`refit=30`) | about 13, which runs without confirmation |
> | Test on a shorter period (later `initial_train_size`, or a larger `fold_stride`) | fewer, depending on the choice |
>
> Daily retraining is the most faithful to "retrain regularly". Weekly or monthly retraining is cheaper and closer to many real schedules.
>
> Which would you like? If you want the full 366-fit run, say so and I'll start it. I'd also suggest adding a `compare` against the seasonal naive baseline, so the accuracy has a reference point.

**Turn 2**

> A 24-hour-ahead forecast would have had a mean absolute error of about 52 users per hour over 2012. That was lower than the seasonal naive baseline's error of about 77.
>
> I ran the monthly-retraining option: 13 model fits, so no cost confirmation was needed.
>
> **How I tested it**
> - **Model:** the server's recommended LightGBM recursive forecaster, with the default lags, rolling-window features and calendar features.
> - **Training and test periods:** I trained on 2011 and tested on all of 2012. That period was my choice, not something you specified.
> - **Folds:** 366 consecutive 24-hour forecasts. The model was retrained every 30 folds (about monthly) on all data up to that point, and used between retrains.
> - **Baseline:** a seasonal naive forecast that repeats past values.
>
> **Results**
>
> | Model | MAE (users/hour) | RMSE (users/hour) |
> |---|---|---|
> | LightGBM recursive | 52.38 | 85.82 |
> | Seasonal naive baseline | 76.76 | 128.68 |
>
> The server reports that LightGBM beats the baseline by 31.8%. For scale, mean hourly users in the data is about 188 and the standard deviation is about 181.
>
> **Caveats**
> - Retraining monthly rather than daily may differ somewhat from retraining every day. I didn't run the daily version (366 fits), so I can't say by how much.
> - I only compared against the baseline, so I can't say whether another estimator or forecaster would do better.
> - The profile and cross-validation setup raised no data problems. The only notice was that RMSE is in the units of the target.
> - I haven't broken the error down by hour of day, day of week or season. The per-fold predictions and metrics are in `out/comparison-5-ce62ff-best-predictions.csv` and `out/comparison-5-ce62ff-best-metrics.csv`.
>
> I can also run the full daily-retrain version if you confirm the 366 fits, or compare other estimators.

### Final answer

**Turn 1**

> I set up the evaluation but haven't run it, because the full version is expensive and I want you to pick the cost.
>
> **Setup:**
> - It forecasts `users` 24 hours ahead with LightGBM through skforecast's recursive forecaster.
> - The first training set is 2011 (up to 2011-12-31).
> - The 2012 test period is 367 back-to-back 24-hour folds.
> - The training window grows as the backtest moves through 2012.
>
> **Cost options:**
> 1. **Retrain every day (367 fits).** This is the closest match to retraining as new data arrives, but it's slow. It needs `confirm_cost: 367`.
> 2. **Retrain weekly (about 53 fits).** The model is refit every 7 folds. It's much cheaper and still reflects regular retraining. It's still just above the 50-fit threshold, so it also needs your confirmation.
> 3. **Retrain every 15 days or so (about 25 fits).** This is cheaper again and runs without a confirmation, but retraining is less frequent.
>
> Which one do you want? If you have no preference, I'd go with weekly. If your production retraining is daily, choose option 1.
>
> I used the server's default plan, and the data has no missing values or irregularities. The plan uses lags and calendar features only, since the CSV has no exogenous columns. The primary metric is MAE.

**Turn 2**

> A 24-hour-ahead forecast would have been off by about 52 bikes per hour on average over 2012. For context, hourly users average about 188 over the two years.
>
> This is a walk-forward backtest. The first model trained on 2011, and each later day was forecast 24 hours ahead. The model was retrained weekly on all data up to that point. That is 367 daily folds covering 2011-12-31 to 2012-12-31, with 8,807 hourly predictions and 53 model fits. Plan: skforecast recursive forecaster with LightGBM, using lags, rolling-window features and calendar features only.
>
> | Metric | Value |
> |---|---|
> | Mean absolute error (MAE) | 51.8 users/hour |
> | Root mean squared error (RMSE) | 85.3 users/hour |
> | Mean absolute scaled error (MASE) | 0.79 |
> | Mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) | 50.3% |
>
> - **MAE vs. RMSE:** RMSE is well above MAE, so the errors vary in size. The MAE and RMSE figures cover all hours together, and I didn't break them down by hour or day.
> - **MAPE:** The 50% figure is a fraction (0.503) converted to a percentage. I wouldn't lean on it. I didn't check why it's high, but MAPE is generally sensitive to hours with very low counts (the minimum is 1).
> - **MASE:** 0.79 is below 1, so the error is smaller than a naive forecast that repeats the previous hour. That isn't a seasonal naive forecast, so it doesn't show the model beats a "same hour yesterday" or "same hour last week" rule. The `compare` tool can test that if you want it.
> - **Retraining frequency:** Retraining was weekly, not daily. A daily retrain would take 367 fits, and I didn't run it.
> - **Data quality:** There were no data problems: no missing values or irregular timestamps.
>
> Files are in `<ws>/out/`:
> - `backtest-5-6ba591-predictions.csv`
> - `backtest-5-6ba591-metrics.csv`

> - **Evaluation:** the first training window is 2011 (up to 2012-01-01). The test period is all of 2012, which is 366 daily folds.
> - **Retraining:** the model refits every fold on an expanding window. That means one fit per day, 366 in total, which matches daily retraining in production.
>
> **Options**
> 1. **Run the full daily retrain (366 fits).** This is the most faithful to production, but it will take a while. I'd pass `confirm_cost: 366`.
> 2. **Retrain weekly (`refit=7`).** This is about 53 fits, which is still slightly above the threshold, so it also needs your confirmation.
> 3. **Retrain every 14 days or monthly.** This is well under 50 fits and quick to run. It's less granular, but it still reflects regular retraining.
> 4. **Score fewer folds** by using a later `initial_train_size` or `skip_folds`.
>
> Which would you like? If you don't have a preference, I'd go with the full daily retrain, since it answers your question most directly.

**Turn 2**

> I ran the backtest with retraining every 14 days. That is 27 fits, instead of the 366 a daily retrain would need. I picked 14 days because a weekly retrain would still have been about 53 fits, above the 50-fit threshold.
>
> **Setup:** LightGBM forecasting 24 hours ahead. The model was first trained on 2011 and then tested on all of 2012 (366 daily folds, 8,783 hourly predictions). It was refit every 14 days on an expanding window of all data up to that point.

> | RMSE | 86.3 users |
> | MAPE | 51.7% |

> - **MASE below 1:** the model had a lower error than a one-step naive forecast (repeat the previous hour). That is a weak benchmark. It is not a seasonal naive forecast like "same hour yesterday", so this run doesn't show whether the model beats that.
>
> **Caveats**
> - These numbers come from refitting every 14 days. Daily retraining, as in your production setup, could score differently. I didn't run it.
> - I didn't tune hyperparameters or compare other models. This is the default plan for the data.
> - The profile and backtest showed no missing values or irregular timestamps in the data.

### Final answer

> I forecast daily sales for 2024-07-19 to 2024-08-01 (14 days) with Chronos-2 small, a pre-trained foundation model. It was the most accurate of the five models I compared.
>
> **Forecast**
> - The predictions run from a minimum of 98.54 to a maximum of 119.79, with a mean of 105.59.
> - The history has a mean of 106 and ranges from 86.36 to 131.4.

>

> - The file has 200 daily observations from 2024-01-01 to 2024-07-18, with no missing values or irregular dates.
> - The forecast is the next 14 days after the last observation. There are no exogenous variables.
>
> **Accuracy**
> I backtested over 5 folds of 14 days each and ranked the models by mean absolute error (MAE):
>
> | Model | MAE |
> |---|---|
> | Chronos-2 small (foundation model) | 3.46 |
> | ARIMA | 3.97 |
> | Direct Ridge | 3.97 |

> | Seasonal naive baseline | 4.85 |
>
> - All four candidates beat the seasonal naive baseline.
> - Chronos-2's root mean squared error was 4.33.
> - Chronos-2 is licensed under Apache-2.0, and it downloads its weights the first time it runs.
> - This forecast of the future has no error measure of its own. The figures above come from the backtest of the same model.

### Final answer

> I forecast daily sales for 2024-07-19 to 2024-08-01 with Chronos-2-small, a pre-trained foundation model. It had the lowest error of the five candidates I compared.
>
> | Date | Forecast | 80% interval (nominal) |
> |---|---|---|
> | 07-19 | 98.7 | 93.2 – 104.7 |
> | 07-20 | 119.8 | 108.4 – 125.7 |
> | 07-21 | 119.7 | 110.6 – 126.0 |
> | 07-22 | 101.3 | 94.9 – 107.3 |
> | 07-23 | 98.6 | 93.1 – 103.8 |
> | 07-24 | 101.1 | 95.2 – 106.9 |
> | 07-25 | 99.9 | 94.4 – 106.0 |
> | 07-26 | 99.8 | 94.0 – 105.7 |
> | 07-27 | 119.1 | 108.2 – 125.3 |
> | 07-28 | 118.7 | 107.9 – 124.2 |
> | 07-29 | 101.0 | 95.3 – 107.0 |
> | 07-30 | 98.5 | 93.3 – 104.1 |
> | 07-31 | 100.8 | 95.2 – 106.4 |
> | 08-01 | 101.0 | 94.9 – 107.1 |
>
> **Data:** The file has 200 daily observations from 2024-01-01 to 2024-07-18. There are no missing values or gaps, and no exogenous columns. I assumed the target column is `sales`, and the profile accepted it.
>
> **Accuracy:** I ran a backtest of 5 folds of 14 days each.
> - **Chronos-2-small:** mean absolute error (MAE) 3.46, the lowest.
> - **Arima:** 3.97.
> - **Direct Ridge:** 3.97.
> - **Recursive Ridge:** 4.69. This is the model the server recommends by default.
> - **Seasonal naive baseline:** 4.85.
> - All 4 models beat the baseline.
> - The forecast itself has no error measure. The MAE figures come from the backtest.
>
> **Interval:** The 80% interval is an estimate. In the backtest, Chronos's interval contained 76.7% of the actual values, a little under the nominal 80%. Its mean width was 11.9 sales units. The recursive Ridge interval covered only 60%, but that model isn't the one used here.
>
> **Notes:**
> - Chronos-2-small is licensed Apache-2.0 and downloads its weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use.
> - The forecast is a single run on all 200 observations. The backtest used 5 windows, so the ranking is based on a small sample.
>
> If you want to reproduce this outside the server, I can fetch the script for it.

### Final answer

> He predicho `Ventas (€)` para los 30 días del 2025-02-04 al 2025-03-05. Los valores diarios están en `<ws>/out/forecast-5-96f4a1-predictions.csv`.
>
> **Predicción**
> - Los valores previstos van de 2.644,5 € a 3.087,8 €, con una media de 2.787,8 €.
> - Usé un modelo LightGBM (`ForecasterRecursive`) con lags diarios, medias móviles y variables de calendario (día de la semana, fin de semana, mes).
> - No pedí intervalo de predicción, así que no hay bandas de incertidumbre.
>
> **Precisión**
> - Hice un backtest con 4 folds de 30 días, entrenando una sola vez con datos hasta 2024-10-06.
> - El error absoluto medio (MAE) fue de 120,3 € y el error cuadrático medio (RMSE) de 150,6 €.
> - El error porcentual medio (MAPE) fue del 4,7 %.
> - El MASE fue 0,746. Eso significa que mejora al pronóstico ingenuo de repetir el valor del día anterior. No lo he comparado con un pronóstico estacional ni con `compare`.
> - La predicción futura en sí no tiene medida de error propia. Las cifras anteriores son las del backtest del mismo plan.
>
> **Qué debes saber**
> - **La columna `Promoción` no se usó.** Es una variable exógena y necesitaría sus valores para los próximos 30 días, que solo puedes darme tú. Si me pasas un CSV con esas fechas y sus valores de promoción, repito el modelo incluyéndola. La predicción actual no refleja ninguna promoción prevista.
> - **Codificación del archivo.** El CSV no está en UTF-8. Lo leí como cp1252, que es lo habitual en Excel de Windows. Los nombres de columna salieron bien, así que no parece haber problema.
> - **Calidad de los datos.** El perfil no detectó huecos de fechas ni valores faltantes.
>
> Si quieres, puedo obtener el script para reproducir el resultado sin el servidor (`get_code`).

### Final answer

> Ya tengo la predicción de `Ventas (€)` para los 30 días siguientes, del 2025-02-04 al 2025-03-05. No usa la columna `Promoción`, porque no tengo sus valores futuros y no los invento. Si me pasas la promoción prevista para esos 30 días en un CSV dentro de `data/`, repito el pronóstico incluyéndola.
>
> **Resultado**
> - Los valores predichos van de 2655 a 3168 €, con una media de 2820 €.
> - El intervalo del 80 % tiene un límite inferior medio de 2757 € y uno superior medio de 2882 €. Es una estimación y no he leído el detalle por día.
> - Los valores día a día están en `out/forecast-8-8c9bd0-predictions.csv`.
>
> **Modelo y precisión**
> - El modelo es Chronos-2 small (licencia Apache-2.0), un modelo preentrenado que no se entrena con tus datos.
> - Lo comparé con otros 5 candidatos en 4 tramos de 30 días y fue el de menor error absoluto medio. Solo 2 de los 5 candidatos superaron al baseline estacional, que repite los valores pasados.
> - El error de la comparación (52,7 €) se midió con un modelo que sí usaba `Promoción`. Al quitarla, volví a medir el mismo plan en esos 4 tramos y dio un error absoluto medio de 47,7 € y un error porcentual medio del 1,9 %.
> - El intervalo del 80 % cubrió el 73,3 % de los valores reales en esa prueba. Es algo menos de lo nominal, así que la incertidumbre real es algo mayor de lo que indican los límites.
> - La predicción del futuro en sí no tiene medida de error propia. Su fiabilidad es la de esas pruebas pasadas.
>
> **Aviso sobre el archivo:** el CSV no está en UTF-8. Lo leí como cp1252, que es lo habitual cuando Excel guarda en Windows. Si ves caracteres raros en los nombres de columna, guárdalo como UTF-8 y lo repito.

>
> **Resumen de la predicción**
> - La media prevista es 2.819,7 €, con un mínimo de 2.655,0 € y un máximo de 3.168,0 €.
> - Los datos son diarios, de 2024-01-01 a 2025-02-03, 400 observaciones.
> - Usé Chronos-2 small, un modelo preentrenado con licencia Apache-2.0. Descarga sus pesos la primera vez que se ejecuta.
> - Salió ganador de una comparación de 6 configuraciones sobre 4 folds de 30 días. Solo 2 de las 5 configuraciones evaluadas (además de la base) superaron al baseline estacional naive: Chronos-2 y ARIMA.
>
> **Precisión medida** (backtest del mismo plan, sin Promoción)
> - El error absoluto medio (MAE) fue de 47,7 €.
> - El error cuadrático medio (RMSE) fue de 59,6 €.
> - El error porcentual medio (MAPE) fue de 1,9 %.

### Final answer

> I forecast 2015-01-02 to 2015-01-15 for stores 101, 102 and 103. The backtest says the forecasts are not clearly better than repeating the previous day's value, so treat them with caution.
>
> **Method**
> - I used one LightGBM model trained on all three stores (`ForecasterRecursiveMultiSeries`), with the server's recommended settings.
> - The data has 400 daily rows per store, from 2013-11-28 to 2015-01-01. It has no gaps or missing values.
> - I took the target to be the `sales` column and the date from the file's date column. I did not check either against the file's headers.
>
> **Forecast, 2015-01-02 to 2015-01-15** (summary statistics from the server; the daily values are in the file)
>
> | Store | Min | Mean | Max |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 101 | 18.56 | 24.53 | 28.96 |
> | 102 | 18.31 | 20.70 | 23.76 |
> | 103 | 17.38 | 20.59 | 22.87 |
>
> The 42 daily predictions (14 per store) are in `out/forecast-5-d72895-predictions.csv`. No prediction interval was requested, so there are none.
>
> **Accuracy**
> This is a 9-fold backtest with 14-day windows. The model was trained once, on data up to 2014-09-03. There was no baseline comparison, which the server does not offer for several series.
>
> | Store | MAE | MASE |
> |---|---|---|
> | 101 | 1.55 | 0.97 |
> | 102 | 3.12 | 1.36 |
> | 103 | 3.68 | 1.01 |
> | Average | 2.78 | 1.11 |
>
> - A MASE below 1 means the error is smaller than that of repeating the previous day's value. Store 101 is just under 1 and store 103 is just over it.
> - Store 102 is the worst, at 1.36.
> - The average MASE is above 1, so on average the model did slightly worse than that one-step reference.
> - The forecast of the future itself has no error measure; the backtest figures above are the best guide to its accuracy.
>
> I haven't run `compare` to test other models, such as a foundation model or other estimators. It is cheap here (27 inference windows), so I can run it if you want.

> I forecast the next 14 days (2015-01-02 to 2015-01-15) for stores 101, 102 and 103. The forecast is less reliable for stores 102 and 103, which the backtest shows a naive forecast would do about as well on or better.
>
> **Method:** I used one LightGBM model shared across the three stores (`ForecasterRecursiveMultiSeries`), with lags 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7, rolling means and calendar features.
>
> **Forecast values** (the model's average prediction over the 14 days):
>
> | Store | Mean | Min | Max |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | 101 | 24.53 | 18.56 | 28.96 |
> | 102 | 20.70 | 18.31 | 23.76 |
> | 103 | 20.59 | 17.38 | 22.87 |
>
> The day-by-day values are in `out/forecast-5-1f886d-predictions.csv`. I didn't read that file, so I haven't described the individual days. I set no prediction interval, so there are no ranges around these numbers.
>

>
> | Store | MAE | MASE |
> |---|---|---|
> | 101 | 1.55 | 0.97 |
> | 102 | 3.12 | 1.36 |
> | 103 | 3.68 | 1.01 |
> | Average | 2.78 | 1.11 |
>
> - **MASE:** the scores compare each store's error to a naive forecast that repeats the previous day's value. Below 1 means better than that naive forecast, and above 1 means worse. This is not a comparison with a seasonal forecast.
> - **Store 101:** only slightly better than the naive forecast.
> - **Store 103:** about the same as the naive forecast.
> - **Store 102:** worse than the naive forecast, and the weakest of the three.
> - **Percentage error:** the average MAPE was 0.165, or 16.5%.

### Final answer

> I've run the backtest, and this is what it showed. I used the default Ridge forecaster (`ForecasterRecursive`) with a 12-month horizon and an 80% interval.
>
> **Setup**
> - `x` has 60 monthly observations, from 2003-07 to 2008-06, with no gaps or missing values.
> - The model trained once on data up to 2006-06. It then forecast 12 months at a time, for two folds that cover 2006-07 to 2008-06 (24 months in total).
>
> **Point accuracy**
>
> | Metric | Value |
> |---|---|
> | Mean absolute error | 0.0631 |
> | Root mean squared error | 0.0852 |
> | Mean absolute percentage error | 0.0696 (about 7.0%) |
> | Mean absolute scaled error | 0.536 |
>
> - The target ranges from 0.56 to 1.26, so the typical miss is about 0.06 in those units.
> - The scaled error is below 1, so the model beat the one-step naive forecast, which repeats the previous value. That is not a seasonal naive forecast. I did not run a comparison against a seasonal baseline.
>
> **80% prediction interval**
> - **Coverage:** 70.8% of the 24 actual values fell inside the interval, below the 80% target.
> - **Width:** the mean interval width was 0.1598, in the units of `x`.
> - **Reading it:** a 12-month interval from this setup should be read as roughly 70% coverage, not 80%.
> - **Small sample:** the first training window left only 24 rows to estimate the intervals. The server warned that intervals tend to be too narrow in that situation.
>
> **Caveats**
> - The backtest has only two folds, so these figures are a rough guide.
> - I didn't open the per-step prediction file, so I can't say how coverage or width vary across the 12 months.
> - The interval method is bootstrapping, and the estimator's hyperparameters were not tuned.
>
> **Next steps**
> - Run a `compare` against the seasonal naive baseline and other models.
> - Produce the actual 12-month forecast beyond 2008-06.
>
> The predictions and metrics are in `out/backtest-4-a73f96-predictions.csv` and `out/backtest-4-a73f96-metrics.csv`.

### Final answer

> I backtested a 12-month forecast of `x` with 80 % prediction intervals. The point forecasts were fairly accurate. The intervals were somewhat too narrow, but only two folds were available, so this is thin evidence.
>
> **Setup**
> - **Data:** 60 monthly observations, 2003-07 to 2008-06, with no missing values or gaps.
> - **Model:** the server's recommended plan, a recursive forecaster using Ridge. Lags are 1–5 and 12, with rolling mean and std features and month and quarter calendar features.
> - **Intervals:** 80 % nominal (10th to 90th percentile), estimated by bootstrapping residuals.
> - **Backtest:** the model was trained once on data up to 2006-06 and then forecast 2006-07 to 2007-06 and 2007-07 to 2008-06. That is 2 folds and 24 actual values.
>
> **Point accuracy (average over the 2 folds)**
>
> | Metric | Value |
> |---|---|
> | MAE | 0.0631 |
> | RMSE | 0.0852 |
> | MAPE | 6.96 % |
> | MASE | 0.536 |
>
> - `x` ranges from 0.56 to 1.26 in the data, with a mean of 0.94.
> - A MASE below 1 means the error was smaller than a one-step "repeat the previous value" forecast on the training data. It does not show the model beats a seasonal naive forecast, because I didn't run a `compare`.
>
> **Interval accuracy**
> - **Coverage:** 70.8 % of the 24 actual values fell inside the intervals, against the 80 % nominal level. That is 17 of 24.
> - **Width:** the mean width was 0.1598, in the units of `x`.
> - **Per-step bounds:** I haven't read them. They are in `out/backtest-4-84a7f6-predictions.csv`.
>
> **Caveats**
> - **Short evidence:** with only 2 folds, 70.8 % versus 80 % is within what chance could produce, so don't read it as a precise coverage figure.
> - **Narrow-interval warning:** the first training window left only 24 residuals to estimate the intervals from. skforecast warns that intervals built from so few residuals tend to be too narrow. The measured coverage is consistent with that, but I can't say that's the cause.
> - **Trained once:** the model was not refit between folds, so the second fold was forecast with a model that had not seen the first fold's year.
>
> If you want, I can run a `compare` against the seasonal naive baseline. It would cost 15 estimator fits, under the 50-fit threshold.

### Final answer

> I forecast `x` for the next 12 months (2008-07 to 2009-06) with Chronos-2 small, and it beat a seasonal-naive baseline in backtesting. The backtest covers only 6 folds, so treat the accuracy figures as rough.
>
> **Forecast**
> - The predictions range from 0.682 to 1.281, with a mean of 1.002.
> - The 80% interval has lower bounds averaging 0.915 and upper bounds averaging 1.088.
> - The month-by-month values are in `out/forecast-6-48ce7e-predictions.csv`. I only used the summary statistics, not the individual rows.
>
> **Accuracy**
> I backtested 6 folds of 12 months each, with the first training window ending 2003-04-01. In each fold the model forecast from the data before it.
>
> | Model | MAE | RMSE | Interval coverage (80% nominal) | Mean interval width |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Chronos-2 small | 0.0570 | 0.0726 | 79.0% | 0.182 |
> | Seasonal naive baseline | 0.0661 | 0.0816 | 75.8% | 0.182 |
>
> - **Baseline comparison:** Chronos-2 had the lower error, and the comparison summary reports it as 13.7% below the baseline's MAE.
> - **Scale:** `x` ranges from 0.336 to 1.257 in the data. The MAE of 0.057 is in the same units.
> - **Interval:** the 80% interval contained 79% of the actual values in the backtest, close to its nominal level.
> - **Forecast itself:** a forecast of the future has no error measure of its own. The figures above are the backtest of the same plan.
>
> **Setup**
> - I chose the foundation model because you asked for one. The server's rules would have recommended Ridge.
> - The model is `autogluon/chronos-2-small` (Apache-2.0 license), and it needs no training.
> - The data had no missing values or date gaps, and no notices came up apart from the license one.
> - I only compared Chronos-2 against the baseline. I did not compare it with Ridge or other models.

### Final answer

**Turn 1**

> **Winner: ForecasterFoundation (Chronos-2 small, `autogluon/chronos-2-small`).** It had the lowest error in the comparison.
>
> I forecast `x` for 12 months, July 2008 to June 2009. The data is monthly, 204 observations from 1991-07 to 2008-06, with no missing values and no exogenous columns. I compared the models over 6 folds of 12 steps each, with initial training up to 2003-04. The cost was 19 estimator fits.
>
> | Rank | Model | MAE | RMSE | MASE |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | 1 | ForecasterFoundation (Chronos-2 small) | 0.0570 | 0.0726 | 0.579 |
> | 2 | ForecasterStats (Arima) | 0.0607 | 0.0790 | 0.616 |
> | 3 | ForecasterRecursive (Ridge) | 0.0620 | 0.0766 | 0.672 |
> | 4 | Baseline (seasonal naive) | 0.0661 | 0.0816 | 0.729 |
> | 5 | ForecasterDirect (Ridge) | 0.0763 | 0.0958 | 0.827 |
>
> - **Ranking:** I ranked by mean absolute error (MAE). Three of the four models beat the seasonal naive baseline. ForecasterDirect did not.
> - **MASE:** This metric is scaled against a one-step naive forecast on the training data, not against the seasonal baseline.
> - **Forecast values:** Over the 12 months the winner's predictions range from 0.682 to 1.281, with a mean of 1.002. The month-by-month values are in `out/forecast-6-a13d3c-predictions.csv`.
> - **Accuracy:** The forecast of the future has no error measure of its own. The error figures above come from the backtest folds.
> - **Model license:** Chronos-2 small is Apache-2.0. It downloads its weights the first time it runs.
> - **Prediction interval:** I didn't request one.
>
> If you want to reproduce this outside the server, I can fetch the script with `get_code`.

**Turn 2**

> I can't tell you why. The comparison only measures which candidate had the lowest error over the folds. It doesn't measure what makes a model better for your data, and I won't guess at a cause.
>
> Here is what was measured, over 6 folds of 12 steps each:
>
> - **MAE:** ForecasterFoundation (Chronos-2 small) had the lowest at 0.0570. ForecasterStats (Arima) followed at 0.0607 and ForecasterRecursive (Ridge) at 0.0620.
> - **RMSE:** ForecasterFoundation was lowest at 0.0726. ForecasterRecursive (Ridge) came next at 0.0766.
> - **MASE:** ForecasterFoundation scored 0.579. A value below 1 means it beat the one-step naive forecast on the training data.
> - **Baseline:** The seasonal naive baseline had an MAE of 0.0661. Three of the four candidates beat it, and ForecasterDirect did not.
>
> The ranking comes from one backtest with 6 folds. It says which model did best on those folds. It doesn't say the model will keep winning on future data.
>
> If you want more evidence, I can run `compare` with a different cross-validation strategy, such as a different `initial_train_size` or a refit in each fold. I can also compare specific configurations that you list. The server doesn't search hyperparameters, so I can only compare candidates you name.

### Final answer

> I did the hyperparameter search for `x` in `data/h2o.csv`, but I can't detect anomalies: the server doesn't do that, so I stopped there.
>
> **Assumptions**
> - You gave no horizon, so I assumed 12 steps (one year of monthly data).
> - I took `x` as the target column. It exists: 204 monthly observations, 1991-07 to 2008-06, no missing values and no notices about the data.
>
> **Hyperparameter search**
> The server has no grid search, so I used `compare`. It backtested 8 candidates I chose by hand, plus a seasonal naive baseline, on the same 6 folds. Each candidate was trained once, starting from 2003-04, and ranked by mean absolute error (MAE).
>
> | Rank | Candidate | MAE |
> |---|---|---|
> | 1 | Ridge, alpha=1 | 0.0620 |
> | 2 | Ridge, alpha=10 | 0.0654 |
> | 3 | Ridge, alpha=0.1 | 0.0654 |
> | 4 | Baseline (seasonal naive) | 0.0661 |
> | 5 | Ridge, alpha=1, lags 1–12 | 0.0668 |
> | 6 | LightGBM, 300 trees, learning rate 0.05 | 0.0803 |
> | 7 | Random forest, 100 trees, depth 5 | 0.0818 |
> | 8 | Random forest, 300 trees, depth 10 | 0.0826 |
> | 9 | LightGBM, 100 trees, learning rate 0.05 | 0.0870 |
>
> - **Best configuration:** Ridge with alpha=1, using the recommended lags [1, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14], window features and month/quarter calendar features.
> - **Against the baseline:** 3 of the 8 candidates beat it (the three Ridge variants with the default lags), and the winner has the lowest error over the folds. Its MASE is 0.672.
> - **How far to trust it:** this is a coarse search, with 8 hand-picked points rather than an exhaustive grid. The ranking only says which candidate had the lowest error over these folds. The server doesn't measure why.
> - **Winning plan:** the best plan is `plan-5-8e913f`.
>
> The server's default plan (Ridge with default settings) wasn't a candidate, so it isn't in the table.
>
> **Anomaly detection**
> The server doesn't detect anomalies. I haven't tried it another way, such as with my own script or by reading the file. If you want that, tell me and I'll do it.
>
> I can also run a forecast of the next 12 months with the winning plan, or widen the search, for example more alpha values or different lags.
